catalog_quote: Suprasegments Tone: Zou language has three contrastive tones. They are: 1. Level, 2. Low-rising, and 3. Falling. Level tone is unmarked, others are marked in ´, ` respectively as in the following: 1. 1 Level : hai “mango” 2. Low-rising : ha´i “chew, masticate/skim off” 3. Falling : ha`i “cup/forget” 2. 1. Level : sa “hot” 2. Low-rising : sa´ “meat” 3. Falling : sa` “dense, thick” ... Conclusion: This paper briefly shows some phonological features of Zou language. ... It is a tonal language having three degree of tones: level, low-rising, and falling.

audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both halves of the deciding quotation are verbatim in the PDF we hold at the stated places (Suprasegments p.16, Conclusion p.17); 'stress'/'accent' absent from the article as claimed. (2) The deciding source is a short 2013 descriptive phonology article; Glottolog lists two PhD reference grammars that outrank it. Both were downloaded now from Shodhganga (an earlier reading's timeouts were the port-8443 redirect; a Referer header bypasses it). Lukram 2013 ch.2 p.36 gives an explicit 'Stress –.. stress, rhythm are not found in this language' plus the same three-tone analysis (its sec. 2.4 is the article's tone section verbatim). Tungdim 2012 ch.4 (JNU, Praat-based) independently analyses Zo as a syllable-TBU tone language with four lexical tones and has no stress/accent section in 767 pp. (3) Coding 'tonal, no word-stress rule, domain unstated' is therefore confirmed

sources.note: First-hand comparative statement: on syllables whose weight falls on the vowel or a sonorant coda, Zo (like Thado, Tedim, Sizang) has three contrastive tones vs four in Mizo and Zahau; they are set up as Tone Categories I (level in Zo), II, and III (falling in all six languages; the Zo TC-III contour sometimes approximates the Tedim one). Stopped syllables without weight on the vowel are generally not tone-bearing (pitch approximates TC-III). Ch.2 shows verbal Form-II derivation in Zo realised largely as a shift to TC-III (grammatical tone); ch.5.3 derives the three categories from Sino-Tibet…
